lines.text: A small land of vineyards between Romania and Ukraine, ruled by princes, tsars and Soviets before finding its own way. This is the story of Moldova.
In the thirteen hundreds the principality of Moldavia was founded east of the Carpathians.
Its greatest prince, Stephen the Great, fought off the Ottomans for decades and built painted monasteries across his land.
In 1436 a small place called Chisinau was first written down. It would grow into the capital.
In 1812 Russia took the land east of the Prut and named it Bessarabia. In 1918 it joined Romania, and in 1940 the Soviets seized it.
Under Soviet rule, the winery of Milestii Mici opened its cellars, which grew into the largest in the world.
Maia Sandu, born in 1972, would become president and lead her country towards the European Union.
As the Soviet Union fell, war broke out on the Dniester, and the east bank, Transnistria, broke away.
On the twenty-seventh of August 1991, Moldova declared its independence.
The new republic was small and poor, and Transnistria has run itself apart ever since.
In 2004 the band O-Zone gave the world Dragostea Din Tei, a summer hit sung in Romanian everywhere.
And in 2024, by the thinnest of margins, Moldovans voted to write the goal of joining the European Union into their constitution.
From Stephen the Great to the door of Europe, Moldova's story is still being written.
